I’ve been struggling for as long as I can remember, but it’s gotten worse lately. I remember being a kid—always fidgety, interrupting others, unable to finish homework. My teachers called me a “chaotic thinker,” and honestly, that never changed. Even now at 56, I can’t sit still during depositions. My mind races nonstop, I talk fast—clients say I overwhelm them. It’s been like this since *before* I was 12.  

About two months ago, things escalated. I felt this surge of energy—I barely slept, maybe three hours a night, but I was wide awake, full of ideas. I poured $50,000 into a real estate venture I didn’t vet. I know it was foolish, but I just *knew* it would pay off. I was restless, snapping at colleagues, pacing my office.  

Then it crashed. For the past three months, I’ve felt hollow. I can’t focus on case files, I lie in bed for hours unable to sleep, and I can’t even pick what to wear. I keep thinking, “Would anyone notice if I just didn’t wake up?” Making decisions feels impossible.  

But the restlessness, the racing thoughts—they didn’t start with the high or the low. They’ve been with me my whole life.
D008-D001_h023.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D008-D001_h024.question:
I’ve struggled with my focus and mood for as long as I can remember, honestly. Even in grade school, my teachers would say I couldn’t sit still, was always blurting out answers, and never finished assignments. That’s never gone away—now at work, I’ll start three coding projects at once, get excited about some new app idea, and pour all my savings into it without thinking it through. I did that last year—blew $20K on a startup idea that lasted two months.  

About two months ago, I went through this intense phase where I barely slept—like, four hours a night but felt wired. Talked so fast my coworker asked if I was on something. I was irritable too—snapped at people over tiny things. But before that, I spent three months just stuck. Couldn’t get out of bed, kept waking up at 3 a.m., mind foggy, like I was thinking through molasses. Some days, I’d stand on the subway platform and get this sudden urge to step forward—no plan, just this urge.  

The difference is, the racing thoughts, the distractibility, the restlessness—they weren’t new during that "high" phase. They’ve been with me since I was a kid. That’s just... me. But when the mood shifts hit, everything gets amplified.
D008-D001_h024.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D008-D001_h025.question:
I’ve been like this as long as I can remember—my wife says even when we met in my twenties, I’d bounce between writing binges, full of energy, barely sleeping, and days where I’d barely get out of bed. But lately, it’s gotten worse. For about two months straight, I was up all night writing, sometimes three books at once, thoughts racing, talking so fast my editor couldn’t keep up. I was impulsive—made inappropriate advances toward a much younger colleague at a literary event, which wasn’t like me at all. Then, just as suddenly, I crashed. For the next three months, I shut everyone out, wouldn’t answer emails, stopped going to readings. I’d sleep eight hours and wake up exhausted. My mind felt foggy—I’d forget where I put my glasses, my notes, even the title of my own manuscript. And there were moments, standing on the balcony of my apartment, where I’d get this sudden, terrifying urge to step off—no plan, just… impulse.

But here’s the thing, doctor: I wasn’t like this only during those highs and lows. I’ve *always* been this way. Since I was a boy, really—I couldn’t sit still in class, always blurting out answers, distracted by every sound. That impulsivity, the restlessness, the rapid speech—it didn’t start with the mania. It never stopped.
D008-D001_h025.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
